The Story of Abstaining from Night Food

I bow to Lord Jina, the word of Jina, and the gurus, and I write the story of one who attained the fruit through abandoning night-time eating.

Those who abandon night eating for the protection of dharma are happy in both worlds, famous, long-lived, radiant, and attain all wealth and peace. But those who eat at night become poor, blind from birth, and are always afflicted by many diseases. They have no children. In the darkness of night, small creatures are not visible and get consumed in food. This causes great sinful bondage — the sin of violence against living beings, the sin of meat-eating. Therefore, abandoning night eating is beneficial for all, and especially for those who do not eat meat. Such righteous shravakas should abstain from food in the morning two ghatis (about 48 minutes) after sunrise and in the evening two ghatis before sunset.

Samantabhadra Swami's view is also the same: 'One who abandons night eating should eat in the morning and evening, leaving two ghatis at the beginning and end.' For those who are not lifelong shravakas, there is no special fault in betel leaf, supari, cardamom, water, and pure medicines. But apart from these, no other grain items, sweets, or fruits should be eaten even in distress.

Those worthy souls who abandon all four types of food at night for their entire life attain the fruit of six months of fasting in a year. Through abandoning night eating, the beloved Kumar attained a wonderful fruit. The detailed story is famous in other texts. Here its essence is written.

In Magadh, Supratishthpur was a famous and prosperous city. It rivalled heaven with its wealth and beauty. Jain dharma was specially propagated there. At the time of this story, its king was Jaysen. Jaysen was knowledgeable in dharma, devoted to policy, and cared for his subjects' welfare.

In that city lived a merchant named Dhanmitra. His wife was Dhanamitra. Both had unbroken love for Jain dharma. One day, after feeding the clairvoyant monk Sagarsen, they asked him, 'Lord, will we have the happiness of a son? If not, then we are tormenting ourselves with vain hope.' The monk, through his clairvoyance, saw that through their merit they would have a son, but if they ate at night, the son would be stillborn. Hearing this, the couple immediately took the vow of never eating at night.

Through the power of this vow, they had a beautiful and virtuous son. The son grew up to be devoted to dharma and ultimately attained liberation. The couple too, through their lifelong observance of this vow, purified their souls and attained liberation.

This story teaches that abstaining from night eating is not merely a dietary rule but a profound spiritual practice that protects all living beings and purifies the soul. The merchant couple's willingness to change their habits for the sake of their future child shows the power of mindful living. The wise should understand that even small acts of self-restraint can have far-reaching spiritual consequences.
